notes.title: Kestrel — scope of work
notes.content:
Endpoint refresh, break-fix, and on-site support at four sites. Standard account resets within the service desk's process.

Explicitly out of scope: privileged accounts, clinical accounts, service accounts, anything touching the clinical network, and anything the service desk has not ticketed.

notes.title: The request I get every month
notes.content:
A clinician, on the floor, at night, locked out of a clinical system, with the manager unreachable. Asks me directly because I am standing there.

The answer is no and the useful part is the second sentence: the on-call manager path exists and I give them the number. Saying only 'I cannot do that' and walking away is how a contractor gets a reputation for being useless, and it is also how the next person just does it.

notes.title: Endpoint refresh — status
notes.content: 640 of 1,100 replaced. The 62 shared workstations on the pilot units are deferred at the client's instruction, which I have flagged twice because the deferred machines are the ones generating tickets.

notes.title: What I see that I should not hold
notes.content:
Field work means standing in clinical areas. I see screens, hear conversations, and get told things because I am physically present and appear harmless.

None of it is mine. I do not record it, repeat it, or act on it, and the fact that nobody would ever know is exactly why the rule has to be absolute.

notes.title: Work orders — April
notes.content: Eleven open, four on site 2, rest across 1 and 4. Nothing on the clinical network because I have no route to it.

notes.title: Client sites — the rota
notes.content:
Four clients, two days a week at the largest, one day each at two others, one day floating.

The floating day is where anything urgent goes and it is never actually floating.

notes.title: Endpoint imaging — the current build
notes.content:
Standard image, six months old, three applications behind current.

Rebuilding the image is a day of work and a week of testing, which is why it drifts and why the drift is always discovered during a refresh.

notes.title: What a field engineer actually does
notes.content:
Roughly a third break-fix, a third deployment, a third things that were not on the work order.

The last third is where the value is and where nobody plans for it.

notes.title: Break-fix patterns
notes.content:
Docking stations, displays, and batteries in that order. Almost never the machine itself.

Half of what gets logged as a laptop fault is a cable.

notes.title: The escort question
notes.content:
Clinical areas need an escort. Getting one can take twenty minutes on a busy ward and often the escort is the person whose device is broken.

Everyone finds this annoying and it exists for good reasons.

notes.title: Access — what I actually have
notes.content:
Standard account resets within the service desk's process, asset records for devices in my work orders, and physical access to non-clinical areas.

That is the whole list. It is deliberately short and I have never needed more, only been asked for more.

notes.title: Contractor versus employee — how it feels
notes.content:
You are in the building every day and you are not on the org chart. People forget which and ask you for things an employee could do.

The good version of this job is knowing exactly where the line is and being useful right up to it.

notes.title: Asset disposal
notes.content:
Devices leaving site need a signed authorisation and certified data destruction.

The number of times someone has asked me to 'just take it' and been surprised by the paperwork is in double figures.

notes.title: Stock at site
notes.content:
Small buffer of spares kept on site — cables, docks, a couple of loaners.

It is not formally inventoried anywhere, which is a problem waiting to be found by an audit.

notes.title: Northgate — my own employer's process
notes.content:
Work orders come from the client's service desk through our dispatch. Anything outside scope goes back to dispatch rather than being agreed on site.

Agreeing scope on site is how contractors end up doing unpaid work and how clients end up with no record of what was done.

notes.title: Handover notes
notes.content:
Every work order closes with what was done and what was found. The 'what was found' part is the useful half and the part most engineers skip.

A loose cable found and mentioned saves someone a ticket next month.

notes.title: Client sites
notes.content: Three managed IT clients, four sites between them. Kestrel is the largest and the most restricted, which suits me.

notes.title: Work order mix
notes.content: Endpoint break-fix, deployments, and on-site support for whatever the remote desk cannot fix. Roughly eleven open at any time.

notes.title: Endpoint refresh — where it stands
notes.content: 640 of 1,100 at Kestrel. Steady pace. The deferred batch is the exception and I have flagged it twice.

notes.title: Imaging and build
notes.content: Standard image, joined and patched before it leaves the bench. The prior image is still on a few hundred machines and it behaves differently in ways nobody has fully catalogued.

notes.title: What contractor scope means in practice
notes.content: Everything I can do is listed in the contract. Anything not listed is out of scope, and urgency does not add to the list. People assume being on site means being authorised and it does not.

notes.title: Being physically present
notes.content: Field work means standing in clinical areas. I see screens, hear conversations, and get told things because I look harmless. None of it is mine. Nobody would ever know, which is exactly why the rule has to be absolute.

notes.title: The remote desk handoff
notes.content: Tickets reach me after the remote desk has tried. About a third are resolved before I arrive and nobody closes them, so I arrive to a fixed problem.

notes.title: Van stock
notes.content: Spare keyboards, mice, docks, cables, and two loan laptops. Whatever is not in the van costs a second visit.

notes.title: Site access
notes.content: Badge access to non-clinical areas at three sites. Clinical areas need an escort. That has never been an obstacle to doing the work.

notes.title: Why I give the on-call number instead of just saying no
notes.content: Refusing without an alternative is how a contractor gets a reputation for being useless, and it is also how the next person just does it themselves.

todos.content: Standing. Refuse AND route — refusing alone is how the next person just does it.

todos.content: The useful half that gets skipped.
